A3.3 Database Programming

SL Unit 6 | DDL, DML, joins, filtering, and updating data

Retrieval Practice

Recall A3.2 before writing SQL.

  1. What does a foreign key do?
  2. Why is a junction table needed in a many-to-many relationship?
  3. Why does 3NF reduce update anomalies?

Press Down for answers

Answer 1

What does a foreign key do?

It links one table to another and helps enforce referential integrity.

Answer 2

Why is a junction table needed in a many-to-many relationship?

It stores the pairs of keys needed to connect many records in one table to many in another.

Answer 3

Why does 3NF reduce update anomalies?

It removes unnecessary duplication, so the same fact does not need updating in multiple places.

SQL language types in the spec

What do DDL and DML stand for, and what do they do?

DDL = Data Definition Language

DDL defines database structures such as tables and fields.

DML = Data Manipulation Language

DML retrieves, adds, changes, or removes rows of data.

Examples on the spec

DDL: CREATE TABLE

DML retrieval: SELECT ... FROM ... WHERE ...

DML updates: INSERT INTO, UPDATE ... SET, DELETE

Constructing SQL queries

Which commands and operators does A3.3.2 expect you to use?

SELECT, DISTINCT, FROM, WHERE

AND, OR, NOT, plus relational operators such as =, >, <, >=, <=, <>

LIKE with the % wildcard and BETWEEN

ORDER BY with ASC and DESC

JOIN to combine two tables

GROUP BY and HAVING when summarizing grouped results

Filtering, matching, and ordering

How do you control which rows appear and how they are sorted?
SELECT DISTINCT Genre
FROM BOOK
WHERE PublishedYear BETWEEN 2015 AND 2024
  AND NOT Genre = 'Archived'
ORDER BY Genre ASC;

WHERE filters rows.

BETWEEN checks an inclusive range.

NOT reverses a condition.

DISTINCT removes duplicates.

ORDER BY sorts the final result.

Queries between two tables with JOIN

How do we show student names from one table and loan records from another?
SELECT s.FirstName, s.LastName, l.LoanDate
FROM STUDENT AS s
JOIN LOAN AS l
    ON s.StudentID = l.StudentID
WHERE l.ReturnStatus = 'On Loan'
ORDER BY l.LoanDate DESC;

JOIN combines the two tables.

ON states the matching key.

WHERE filters after the join.

ORDER BY sorts the result.

Grouped query results

What do GROUP BY and HAVING do in A3.3.2?
SELECT TutorGroup, COUNT(*) AS LoanCount
FROM STUDENT AS s
JOIN LOAN AS l
    ON s.StudentID = l.StudentID
GROUP BY TutorGroup
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2
ORDER BY LoanCount DESC;

GROUP BY puts rows into categories.

COUNT(*) summarizes each group.

HAVING filters whole groups after the summary is calculated.

Updating data with SQL

How does SQL add, change, and remove records?

INSERT INTO adds a new record.

UPDATE ... SET changes existing data.

DELETE removes data.

Use a WHERE clause so only the intended rows are changed.

INSERT INTO STUDENT (StudentID, FirstName, LastName)
VALUES (1026, 'Samira', 'Ali');
UPDATE STUDENT
SET LastName = 'Chen-Wong'
WHERE StudentID = 1025;
DELETE FROM LOAN
WHERE LoanID = 4008;

Performance when updating indexed columns

Why can some updates be slower than others?

An index is an extra structure used to speed up searching and sorting.

If you update a column that is indexed, the database may also need to update the index.

After large numbers of changes, indexes may need to be rebuilt or reorganized to restore performance.

Exam link: A3.3.3 is not only about the SQL commands. It also includes the performance implications of heavy data modification.

Key Takeaways

  • DDL = Data Definition Language: defines structures such as tables.
  • DML = Data Manipulation Language: retrieves and changes rows of data.
  • A3.3.2 expects joins, filtering, relational operators, pattern matching, ordering, grouping, and group filters.
  • A3.3.3 expects INSERT INTO, UPDATE ... SET, DELETE, plus the effect of updates on indexed columns.
